What this data says

  • Load 'baby': gravel gave the highest median vertical vibration (0.68 m/s², n=1), 2.7× smooth asphalt (0.25 m/s², n=1).
  • Load 'rice_5kg': cobblestones gave the highest median vertical vibration (1.07 m/s², n=4), 8.8× indoor floor (0.12 m/s², n=4).
  • Load 'rice_5kg', on the 4 surface(s) all strollers share: Stroller A (air tyres) 0.33, Stroller B (foam tyres) 0.51 m/s² median vertical.
  • 12 of 19 walks reached a total value of 0.315 m/s² or more, where ISO 2631-1 Annex C stops calling vibration 'not uncomfortable' for adults.
  • 7 walk(s) cross an ISO 2631-1 limit (crest factor > 9, MTVV/a_w > 1.5 or VDV ratio > 1.75) beyond which RMS alone may understate peaks; quote MTVV and VDV alongside a_wz for those.

Small samples: treat differences as leads to test with more repeats, not conclusions.

Method

  • Phone accelerometer recordings (phyphox, 'Acceleration with g') are resampled to a uniform rate. The part where the phone lay still in its walk orientation is found from the direction of gravity; handling at both ends is cut, plus a few seconds of margin.
  • Axes are rotated so z is perpendicular to the surface the phone lies on. Vertical (z) is weighted with Wk, horizontal (x, y) with Wd (ISO 2631-1:1997, Annex A, exact analogue responses applied in the frequency domain).
  • Stops (no vibration above 2 Hz for 3 s or more) are excluded from RMS values, so a wait at a crossing doesn't dilute the result.
  • a_wz: frequency-weighted RMS vertical acceleration. a_v: vibration total value, √(a_wx² + a_wy² + a_wz²). MTVV: worst 1-second running RMS. VDV: vibration dose value (grows with duration, sensitive to shocks). Crest: peak ÷ RMS; past 9, RMS alone may understate peaks.

Caveats

  • There is no vibration standard for infants. ISO 2631-1 and its Annex C comfort bands describe adults; they are used here only as a common reference scale, as in published stroller studies.
  • Annex C bands formally apply to the total value a_v; the comparison chart shows the vertical a_wz against them because vertical vibration dominates in strollers.
  • Phones typically sample at 100–500 Hz. At 100 Hz, content above 50 Hz is not captured (the ISO band extends to 80 Hz).
  • A phone on the mattress measures the mattress near the baby, not the baby's body. Runs with the phone under a 5 kg load measure the body-mattress interface, closer to ISO seat-pad practice.
  • Phone accelerometers are not calibrated instruments. The report checks each phone's reading of gravity (should be 9.81 m/s²).
